title: This, that, and more than one
goal: Point to things and people with یہ and وہ, make nouns plural, and use Urdu's eight question words.
bekal: point at something and ask what or who it is
form the plural of the four groups of nouns
use کیا، کون، کہاں، کب، کیوں، کیسے، کتنا، کون سا

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — عائشہ کے گھر میں
dialogs.intro: Ayesha invites Budi into her family's home. A large photo hangs on the living-room wall.

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: بودی، یہ میرا گھر ہے۔ اندر آئیے!
lines.baca: Būdī, ye merā ghar hai. andar āiye!
lines.id: Budi, this is my home. Please come in!
lines.literal: Budi, this my house is. inside come-please!

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: بہت خوبصورت گھر ہے۔ یہ تصویر کیا ہے؟
lines.baca: bahut ḵūbsūrat ghar hai. ye tasvīr kyā hai?
lines.id: It's a beautiful house. What's this picture?
lines.literal: very beautiful house is. this picture what is?

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: یہ میرے والد ہیں، اور یہ میری والدہ ہیں۔
lines.baca: ye mere vālid haiñ, aur ye merī vālida haiñ.
lines.id: This is my father, and this is my mother.
lines.literal: this my-(pl) father are, and this my-(f) mother are.

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: یہ میرے بھائی ہیں۔ ان کے نام حسن اور عمر ہیں۔
lines.baca: ye mere bhāī haiñ. un ke nām Hasan aur Umar haiñ.
lines.id: These are my brothers. Their names are Hasan and Umar.
lines.literal: these my brothers are. them of names Hasan and Umar are.

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: وہ میری کتابیں ہیں۔ اردو ادب بہت دلچسپ ہے۔
lines.baca: vo merī kitābeñ haiñ. urdū adab bahut dilchasp hai.
lines.id: Those are my books. Urdu literature is fascinating.
lines.literal: those my-(f) books are. Urdu literature very interesting is.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: یہ کمرہ بہت بڑا ہے۔ وہ دروازہ کہاں جاتا ہے؟
lines.baca: ye kamra bahut baṛā hai. vo darvāza kahāñ jātā hai?
lines.id: This room is huge. Where does that door go?
lines.literal: this room very big is. that door where going-is?

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: وہ باورچی خانہ ہے۔ چائے تیار ہے!
lines.baca: vo bāvarchī-ḵāna hai. chāe taiyār hai!
lines.id: That's the kitchen. The tea is ready!
lines.literal: that cook-house is. tea ready is!

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: بہت بہت شکریہ۔ آپ کا خاندان بہت مہربان ہے۔
lines.baca: bahut bahut shukriya. āp kā ḵāndān bahut mehrbān hai.
lines.id: Thank you so much. Your family is very kind.
lines.literal: very very thanks. you of family very kind is.

notes: **Two words cover four jobs.** The word یہ means "this" and also "he/she (nearby)"; وہ means "that" and also "he/she (farther away)". And neither **changes for the plural**: یہ کتاب ہے ("this is a book") and یہ کتابیں ہیں ("these are books") both use یہ. The plural shows up in the noun and in ہیں at the end.

**A practical rule for یہ or وہ.** If you can touch or point at the thing or person from where you stand, use یہ. Anything farther — across the room, in a photo, in another city, or just mentioned in conversation — use وہ. For a third person who isn't present, وہ is almost always right.

**Why میرے والد and not میرا والد?** Because for parents, in-laws, and anyone you respect, Urdu uses **the plural as a mark of respect** — just as آپ is actually plural. So "my father" is میرے والد ہیں, literally "my fathers are", even though there's only one. Using the singular for والد sounds disrespectful.

**Whose? — کس کی.** The word کون ("who") turns into کس as soon as a postposition attaches to it, your first example of the **oblique form** covered in unit 6. For now, memorize two ready-made sentences: یہ کس کا ہے؟ ("whose is this?", for a masculine thing) and یہ کس کی ہے؟ (for a feminine thing).

**Pakistani homes have charming names for their rooms.** The word باورچی خانہ (*bāvarchī-ḵāna*) literally means "the cook's house" = kitchen. The pattern خانہ ("house, place") repeats in lots of words: کتب خانہ (library), غسل خانہ (bathroom), ڈاک خانہ (post office), کارخانہ (factory). Once you spot خانہ, half of all place names read themselves.

**Welcoming a guest: اندر آئیے.** Literally "please come inside". The polite command ends in ـیے, and you'll hear it constantly: بیٹھیے (please sit), کھائیے (please eat), سنیے (please listen), معاف کیجیے (please excuse). Unit 16 covers all the command forms; for now, just recognize the pattern.

grammars.title: Making plurals: four groups, and that's all
body: Every Urdu noun falls into one of the four groups below, and you can tell the group from the shape of the word itself. There's no fifth group and no exception you need to worry about at A1.
after: ⚠️ The second group is the most common source of confusion: گھر can mean "house" or "houses", and only the verb tells you which. یہ گھر بڑا ہے = one house. یہ گھر بڑے ہیں = several houses. Notice ہے versus ہیں, and the adjective changing along with it.

Nouns borrowed from Arabic often bring their own plurals, and these are still used: the plural of کتاب can be کتب, the plural of حال is حالات, and the plural of خبر is اخبار — the word that came to mean "newspaper". You don't need to form them yourself, just recognize them when reading.

grammars.title: Eight question words
body: Urdu puts the question word **right before the verb**, not at the start of the sentence as English does. آپ کہاں جاتے ہیں؟ = "you where going are?". The rest of the sentence stays as it is.
after: ⚠️ **The difference between کون and کون سا.** The word کون asks about people: وہ کون ہے؟ ("who is he?"). The phrase کون سا asks you to choose between things: کون سی کتاب اچھی ہے؟ ("which book is good?"). Notice that کون سا changes for gender — کون سا لڑکا · کون سی کتاب · کون سے لڑکے — because it ends in ـا.
The question word کتنا changes too: کتنا پانی؟ (how much water), کتنی چائے؟ (how much tea), کتنے لوگ؟ (how many people).

blocks.title: Three nouns whose gender is often guessed wrong
items: The word میز (table) ends in a consonant, so instinct says masculine — but it's **feminine**: میز صاف ہے and میزیں صاف ہیں. It's a Persian word, and Persian words ending in a consonant are often feminine.
The word پانی (water) ends in ـی, so instinct says feminine — but it's **masculine**: پانی ٹھنڈا ہے. Its equally tricky cousins: آدمی (man, m), موتی (pearl, m), گھی (ghee, m).

The word کھانا (food) ends in ـا, so it's masculine — and that's right. The trap: it's also the verb "to eat". کھانا اچھا ہے = "the food is good", while کھانا کھانا = "to eat food", the same word twice in a row, and that's perfectly normal Urdu.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with یہ or وہ, following the hint in brackets.
items: ____ میرا گھر ہے۔ (you're standing in front of it)
____ کمرہ بہت بڑا ہے۔ (you're standing in it)
وہ ____ ہے؟ — وہ میرا بھائی ہے۔
آپ ____ ہیں؟ — میں گھر میں ہوں۔

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: یہ کیا — کون — کہاں — کون — کتنے کا
یہ میری کتابیں ہیں۔ — وہ کون ہے؟ — یہ کمرہ بہت بڑا ہے۔ — یہ لڑکے کون ہیں؟ — یہ ہمارا خاندان ہے۔
wave: Before you start unit 4, point at ten things in your room and say یہ … ہے for each one. If you don't know a word's gender yet, write it down.
